title: Weighing & Balancing
strapline: Which side goes down? Balance pans, heavy stones and the question of how much things really weigh.
intent: Balance scales make weight visible — one side dips, the other rises — giving children a concrete, testable way to compare heavy and light.
Predicting which of two objects is heavier, then checking on the scales, is genuine scientific comparison, and children are often surprised.
Loading, adjusting and reading the pans builds fine-motor control and an early, physical sense of equal, more and less.
The activity is rich in comparative language — heavier, lighter, the same, balanced — grounded in what children can see and feel.
Working towards a level balance is an absorbing, self-correcting problem that invites persistence and adjustment.
It lays honest foundations for measuring and for the mathematical idea of equivalence, all through play.
implementation: Offer sturdy balance scales and a rich mix of objects — conkers, pebbles, pinecones, metal spoons, feathers, and non-standard weights like acorns.
Ask for a prediction first: 'which do you think is heavier — the big pinecone or the little stone?' — then test it.
Welcome the surprises: 'the small one was heavier! What do you think is inside it?'
Set balancing challenges: 'how many acorns balance this stone?', 'can you make both sides the same?'
Model the comparative words as the pans move, and let children start to describe what they see.
Link it to the kitchen and shop — weighing flour to bake, weighing fruit on the market stall — so weight has real jobs.
key_questions: Which do you think is heavier — the big pinecone or the little stone?
The small one was heavier! What do you think is inside it?
How many acorns balance this stone?
Can you make both sides the same?
Which side goes down, and what does that tell us?

Children use comparative language grounded in what they see and feel — heavier, lighter, the same, balanced.
Children work towards a level balance — an absorbing, self-correcting problem inviting persistence.
Children lay foundations for measuring and the idea of equivalence, all through play.

Non-standard weights like acorns for 'how many balance this?' challenges.

playing_exploring: Children load and reload the pans, testing object after object to see which way they tip.

active_learning: Children persist at getting the pans to balance, adjusting a little at a time until they are level.
creating_thinking: Children predict which is heavier, test it, and are prompted to rethink when a small object turns out to weigh more.
